Let me recall the classic Euclid-style argument adapted to primes of the form 4k+3.

Suppose finitely many: p1, ..., pk. Let N = 4(p1...pk) - 1. N is congruent to 3 mod 4. A product of primes that are all 1 mod 4 is 1 mod 4, so N has a prime factor q that is 3 mod 4. q cannot be any pi because N leaves remainder -1 on division by each pi. Contradiction.

content.text: Yes. Assume there are only finitely many such primes p1, ..., pk and set N = 4·p1·…·pk − 1. N ≡ 3 (mod 4), so at least one prime factor q of N is ≡ 3 (mod 4), because products of primes ≡ 1 (mod 4) are ≡ 1 (mod 4). But q cannot equal any pi, since each pi leaves remainder −1 when dividing N. This contradiction shows there are infinitely many primes p with p mod 4 = 3.
